title: Cao Zhi's Seven-Step Poem
text:
Cao Cao, the great warlord of the end of the Han dynasty, had several talented sons. For a time he seemed to favor Cao Zhi, a brilliant poet, as his heir, but in the end he chose the elder, Cao Pi. When Cao Cao died in 220, Cao Pi took the throne as the first emperor of Wei. He never trusted his gifted brother.

The New Account of Tales of the World, a collection of anecdotes compiled in the fifth century by Liu Yiqing, tells what happened next. The emperor ordered Cao Zhi to compose a poem in the time it took to walk seven steps. If he failed, he would be put to death.

Cao Zhi walked and composed. His poem compared the two brothers to beans and beanstalks. The beans are boiled to make a soup, he said, while the stalks burn under the pot; the beans weep in the pot. We sprang from the same root, so why are you in such a hurry to cook me?

According to the story, the emperor was deeply ashamed. Cao Zhi's life was spared. He spent the rest of it moved from one fief to another under close watch, kept away from any real power, and died in 232 at forty. The line about "the same root" became a proverb, used ever since to plead against quarrels between brothers and kin.
lesson: Rivalry between siblings can be shamed by a reminder of what they share. Before attacking family, remember that you grew from the same root.
people: Cao Pi (Emperor Wen of Wei), Cao Zhi
source: Liu Yiqing, Shishuo Xinyu (A New Account of Tales of the World), Literature section 66
caveat: The story appears centuries later and historians doubt it happened; the poem may not be Cao Zhi's own.
